Name: Nabakalebara
Description / Significance: The periodic ritual replacement of the wooden deities at Puri, conducted once every 12–19 years according to a lunar calendar rule, involving the ceremonial transfer of a sacred, unseen substance (Brahma Padartha) from the old idols to the new ones.

Name: Chhera Pahara
Description / Significance: The Gajapati king's ceremonial sweeping of the chariots during Rath Yatra with a golden-handled broom, a ritual act symbolizing that before Jagannath, king and commoner are equal.

Name: Suna Vesha
Description / Significance: The golden-attire adornment ritual for the deities, drawing massive crowds during the Rath Yatra period as the idols are dressed in elaborate gold ornaments atop their chariots.

Name: Anasara
Description / Significance: The 14-day period following Snana Yatra when the deities are believed to have fallen ill from their ritual bath and are secluded from public view, during which they're symbolically "treated" with herbal remedies.

Name: Mahaprasad Tradition
Description / Significance: The temple's communal kitchen, one of the largest in the world, cooks food for thousands daily using earthen pots stacked over open fire — a cooking method essentially unchanged for centuries.

Name: Rukuna Rath Yatra
Description / Significance: A separate chariot festival tradition observed for local deities distinct from the main Puri Rath Yatra, reflecting how the chariot-procession format extends beyond Jagannath worship alone.

Name: Debasnana Purnima
Description / Significance: The formal name for the ritual bathing ceremony forming the basis of Snana Yatra, using exactly 108 pots of consecrated water poured over the deities.

Name: Nuakhai Bhetghat
Description / Significance: The greeting and reconciliation custom observed alongside Nuakhai, where family and community disputes are traditionally set aside and relationships renewed.

Name: Sal Puja
Description / Significance: A tribal ritual centered on worship of the sal tree, reflecting the deep ecological relationship between tribal communities and their forest environment.

Name: Chait Parab
Description / Significance: A spring ritual observed among western Odisha's tribal communities marking seasonal transition and agricultural renewal.

Name: Karamsani
Description / Significance: A ritual associated with worship of the Karam tree among western Odisha's tribal communities, tied to prosperity and protection of family members.

Name: Kandhen Budhi Yatra Ritual
Description / Significance: A ceremonial tribal worship tradition of the Kondh community, centered on earth and ancestor veneration.

Name: Niyamgiri Sacred-Hill Tradition
Description / Significance: The Dongria Kondh's religious and ecological reverence for the Niyamgiri hills as the abode of their deity Niyam Raja, a belief system that became globally known through their resistance to bauxite mining on the site.

Name: Bonda Tribal Customs
Description / Significance: The distinctive dress, ornamentation, and social customs of the Bonda community of Malkangiri district, considered one of India's most isolated and culturally distinct tribal groups.

Name: Santhal Dance-Music Tradition
Description / Significance: Music and dance central to the social and ceremonial life of the Santhal community, India's third-largest tribal group, historically also tied to their resistance during British rule.

Name: Gond Warrior Heritage
Description / Significance: Customs and oral traditions of the Gond community across Koraput, Balangir, and Kalahandi, reflecting their historical identity as one of South Asia's largest tribal groups.

Name: Bhumia Marriage Customs
Description / Significance: Distinctive marriage rituals of the Bhumia community, considered among the more unique tribal marriage traditions documented in the state.

Name: Oraon Agricultural Tradition
Description / Significance: Farming and tea-plantation-linked customs of the Oraon community, considered among the more economically integrated tribal traditions in Odisha.

Name: Boita Bandana Ritual
Description / Significance: The ceremonial floating of miniature boats made of paper, leaves, or bark to honor ancestral sailors, performed by families on the banks of rivers and tanks during Kartik Purnima.

Name: Chhau Ritual Martial Tradition
Description / Significance: The ceremonial and martial-training roots underlying the Mayurbhanj Chhau performance, historically connected to physical preparation for royal guards.

Name: Sitalsasthi Procession
Description / Significance: The enacted marriage procession of Shiva and Parvati through the streets of Bhubaneswar, with local community members formally playing family roles in the ceremony.

Name: Jhoti/Chita Floor Art
Description / Significance: Ritual rice-paste floor and threshold painting done by women for auspicious occasions, functioning as both decoration and a symbolic invitation to deities.

Name: Danda Yatra
Description / Significance: A Shaivite penance festival involving real physical austerities such as walking on hot coals or piercing rituals, performed by devotees fulfilling vows.

Name: Grama Devi (Village Deity) Worship
Description / Significance: A widespread localized tradition where individual villages maintain their own protective deity, worshipped independently of the larger temple network.

Name: Khond Earth-Centered Ritual Tradition
Description / Significance: Rituals honoring land, ancestors, and lineage among the Khond community, considered the most widespread tribal group in the Eastern Ghats region of Odisha.

Name: Bhitarkanika Fishing Community Traditions
Description / Significance: Customs and livelihood practices tied to the mangrove-linked fishing lifestyle of communities living around the Bhitarkanika wetlands.

Name: Chhatisha Niyog
Description / Significance: The Puri Jagannath temple's traditional system of 36 categories of ritual service providers, each hereditarily responsible for a specific temple duty, forming one of the most elaborate ritual labor divisions in Indian temple practice.

Name: Ratha Nirmana
Description / Significance: The annual craft-ritual tradition of building the Rath Yatra chariots entirely from scratch each year using specified wood and measurements, a process that itself functions as a religious observance.

Name: Community Grain-Offering Ritual
Description / Significance: The agricultural offering custom at the heart of Nuakhai in western Odisha, where the year's first rice harvest is ritually offered to the local deity before being consumed by anyone in the community.

Name: Kapdaganda Weaving Tradition
Description / Significance:
The generational transmission of Dongria Kondh shawl-weaving knowledge from mother to daughter, functioning as both a craft practice and a living record of community identity and cosmology.
